title: High-strength dual-phase steel produced through fast-heating annealing method
abstract: Fast-heating annealing method provides a new possibility to produce high-performance dual-phase (DP) steel by controlling austenite decomposition upon cooling. A quenching dilatometer with programmable heating-holding-cooling cycles was employed to stimulate the fast-heating annealing process of a cold-rolled dual-phase steel in the present work. Electron probe microanalysis and X-ray diffraction were conducted to reveal the microstructural evolution and phase transformation behavior in combination with dilatometric measurements. Experimental results showed that in case the cold-rolled DP980 steel sheet was rapidly austenitized just above the full austenitization temperature at a heating rate of 300 ​K/s, ultrafine and discontinuous martensite surrounded by interconnected network ferrite could be obtained after holding at 1073 ​K for 100 ​s. A phase transformation model was established for the cold-rolled dual-phase steel subjected to fast-heating annealing treatment. The produced fast-heating DP980 steel sheet possessed an ultimate tensile strength of about 1200 ​MPa and a fracture elongation up to 16.7%.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Advanced high-strength steels, mainly including transformation-induced plasticity steels, complex-phase steels, martensitic steels and dual-phase steels, are numerously applied in automobile manufacturing owing to their desirable formability, high strength and light weight [ 1 , 2 ]. Transformation-induced plasticity steels, consisted of retained austenite in a ferritic matrix and a small portion of bainite and/or martensite, are suitable for automotive structural and safety parts like cross members, longitudinal beams, reinforcements, sills and bumper reinforcements by taking advantage of their excellent energy absorption capacity [ 3–6 ]. Complex-phase steels are composed of small amounts of martensite, retained austenite and pearlite in a ferritic or bainitic matrix with high ultimate tensile strength, which are mainly used for parts requiring good impact resistance [ 7–9 ]. Martensitic steels are characterized by a martensitic matrix with small amounts of ferrite and/or bainite, which would demonstrate adequate formability at extremely high strength by proper post-quenching [ 10–13 ]. Dual-phase steels containing ferrite and martensite are commonly used for automotive body panels, wheels and bumpers due to their excellent mechanical properties and good deformability [ 14–18 ]. Presently, continuous annealing process with low heating rates of 3–10 ​K/s is widely applied for large-scale industrial production. The phase constituents, morphologies and distribution are closely linked to the annealing process parameters, including heating rate, holding temperature/time, and cooling rate as well. Generally, the austenitization starts in an almost fully-recrystallized ferritic matrix, and nucleation of austenite occurs preferentially at the interfaces between ferrite and cementite, as shown in a lot of efforts made [ 19–23 ]. For example, Zeytin et al. [ 19 ] found that the effect of holding time was dependent on the chemical compositions when they annealed several different grades of commercial low-alloy steels at a constant intercritical temperature. Mohanty et al. [ 20 ] found that the heating rate affected the austenite formation not only during continuous heating, but also during isothermal holding, and the effect was more pronounced at lower annealing temperatures. The austenite formation and its distribution were strongly influenced by the overlapping extent between the processes of recrystallization and austenitization.

Fast-heating annealing process with a heating rate higher than 100 ​K/s was developed during the past decades. Different from the conventional continuous annealing process, a mass of grain boundaries and unreleased distortion energy within the cold-rolled microstructure may be reserved and thus abundant of potential sites would be available for nucleation during fast-heating annealing process. Consequently, the kinetics of ferrite recrystallization, nucleation and growth mechanism of austenite would change greatly [ 24–31 ]. For example, Xu et al. [ 29 ] observed higher heating rate of 500 ​K/s produced more austenite for a constant annealing time of 80 ​s when a transformation-induced plasticity steel was held at 1073 ​K; meanwhile, it resulted in a larger volume fraction of retained austenite (RA) containing lower carbon content in comparison to the lower heating rate of 5 ​K/s. Liu et al. [ 30 ] reported a heating rate of 300 ​K/s led to an accelerated transformation with refined austenite in a quenching and partitioning (Q&P) steel. Bainite transformation was completely suppressed during the partitioning process and more martensite/austenite (M/A) islands formed. The ultimate tensile strength was found to be 90 ​MPa (~10%) higher than that of the conventional annealed specimens (5 ​K/s). Very recently, ultra-high heating rate up to 1500 ​K/s was employed by Cerda et al. [ 31 ] in cold-rolled carbon steels, and they observed striking grain refinement after ultrafast heating. Furthermore, they found that the variation of mechanical properties with the heating rate correlated primarily with the qualitative increase of the ferrite and bainite. As described above, industrial production of high-strength dual-phase steel is mostly performed through slow-heating intercritical annealing. In the present work, we employed the fast-heating (300 ​K/s) annealing method in a cold-rolled DP980 dual-phase steel sheet, and the main objective is to clarify the phase transformation behavior so as to explore the possibility to produce high-strength steel by controlling austenite decomposition.

sections.heading: Experimental procedure
paragraphs:
An industrially 80% cold-rolled DP980 steel sheet of 1.0 ​mm thickness was investigated in the present study, and the chemical composition was given in  Table 1 
                      . Rectangular sheet specimens with dimensions of 4.0 ​mm ​× ​10 ​mm ​× ​1.0 ​mm were wire-cut along the rolling direction and then mechanically polished for fast-heating annealing treatment ( Fig. 1 
                      a). Bone-like tensile specimens ( Fig. 1 b) were further wire-cut from the rectangular specimens subjected to fast-heating treatment. The austenitization temperatures ( Ac 
                      1  ​= ​1034 ​K,  Ac 
                      3  ​= ​1093 ​K) for the studied cold-rolled DP980 steel sheet at a heating rate of 300 ​K/s were determined through dilatometric measurement (TA DIL 805L), as shown in  Fig. 2 
                      a. A martensitic transformation ( M

                       ​= ​625 ​K) occurred upon cooling at 70 ​K/s ( Fig. 2 b). The DIL 805L quenching dilatometer with programmable heating-holding-cooling cycles was used to stimulate the fast-heating annealing treatment. The rectangular sheet specimen was firstly induction heated to 1123 ​K (~30 ​K above the  Ac 
                      3 ) with a preset heating rate of 300 ​K/s, followed by cooling (25 ​K/s) to 1073 ​K wherein they were held for 50 ​s or 100 ​s, respectively. Subsequently, the specimen underwent a stepped cooling from 1073 ​K to 943 ​K first at a cooling rate of 15 ​K/s and then to 513 ​K ​at a cooling rate of 70 ​K/s by purging nitrogen gas. All specimens were overaged at 513 ​K for 300 ​s and lastly furnace cooling to room temperature. Hereafter both groups of specimens with different holding time were referred as FH-50 and FH-100, respectively. The temperature data was acquired by a spot welded  K -type thermocouple at the steel surface in the present study.

Microstructure, fracture morphology and elemental analyses were performed using an electron probe microanalyzer (EPMA-8050G) equipped with a wavelength-dispersive spectrometer (WDS). X-ray diffraction (XRD Dlmax-2500) with Cu  K 
                      
                         α 
                       radiation was conducted to detect the phase and crystal structure with a scanning rate of 1°/min. Tensile tests at least 5 specimens for each group were conducted under displacement control at a strain rate of 1 ​× ​10 −4  s −1  using a servo hydraulic tabletop test system (MTS Bionix 370.02). The hardness measurements were conducted using a Vickers hardness method using 500 gf load with a dwell time of 15 ​s (MVS-1000Z). The Vickers hardness was determined by averaging at 20 readings.

sections.heading: Results and discussion
paragraphs:
Backscattered electron image of the initial cold-rolled DP980 dual-phase steel sheet is shown in  Fig. 3 
                      a, which is composed of deformed dark ferrite and light pearlite. The pearlite colonies and ferrite elongated along the rolling direction. Part of pearlite is crushed and bended in the colonies, and some broken particles are inlaid in the deformed ferrite grain boundaries in a line intermittently, as indicated by red arrows in  Fig. 3 b. Electron probe microanalyses on the elemental distributions corresponding to the scanning image of  Fig. 3 a reveal that the pearlite colonies contain more carbon (C), whereas both manganese (Mn) and silicon (Si) elements homogeneously distribute within the measured area.

Fig. 4 
                      a gives two temperature-time curves with 50 ​s and 100 ​s holding time at 1073 ​K, respectively, and the corresponding dilatometric data. Enlarged image at the fast-heating stage (from point  o  to  a ) is shown in  Fig. 4 b. One can see that at the early fast-heating stage, the dilatometric curves almost increase linearly with a thermal expansion coefficient of ~1.84 ​× ​10 −5  ​K −1  following a constant heating rate of 300 ​K/s, and slightly falls down above 933 ​K with a coefficient of ~1.70 ​× ​10 −5  ​K −1 , which are generally ascribed to the recovery and recrystallization of deformed ferrite, respectively [ 32 , 33 ]. With further increasing temperature higher than 1034 ​K ( Ac 
                      1 , point  a ), a clear volume shrinkage corresponding to the formation of austenite happens. At the peak temperature of 1123 ​K (point  b , higher than the  Ac 
                      3 ), the specimens should be fully austenitized since the dilatometric curves show slight pulling-up above the  Ac 
                      3  (1093 ​K). Meanwhile, it should be noticed that with the commence of transformation from ferrite to austenite, the actual heating rate decreased dramatically to ~65 ​K/s due to large magnetic discrepancy existed between austenite and ferrite (electromagnetic induction heating). The volume shrinkage with fluctuation feature during subsequent cooling to 1073 ​K (from point  b  to  c ) may be resulted from the overlapping of austenite decomposition. During isothermal holding at 1073 ​K (from point  c  to  d ), more ferrites form by austenite decomposition corresponding to the linear expansion. When rapidly cooling to 513 ​K from point  d  to  f  (113 ​K below the  M 
                      f ), residual austenite transforms to martensite and results in a volume expansion, as seen from the circled image in  Fig. 4 a. The specimen keeps almost constant during overaging at 513 ​K (from point  f  to  g ).

In order to verify the speculation described above, microstructure characterization and elemental distribution on both groups of specimens were conducted, as shown in  Fig. 5 
                      . The following results are obtained: (1) different from the blocky martensite in the FH-50 specimen ( Fig. 5 a), discontinuous and ultrafine island-like martensite was observed in the FH-100 specimen ( Fig. 5 c). According to the SEM quantitative microstructure analysis, it was found that about 64.0% and 54.5% of martensite formed in the FH-50 and FH-100 specimens, respectively. The microstructure refined clearly in the FH-100 specimen in contrast to that in the FH-50 specimen; (2) both groups of specimens consisted of martensite, ferrite, retained austenite (RA) and/or martensite-austenite islands (M/A), as marked in the enlarged scanning images ( Fig. 5 b,d), one can distinguish that decomposition of lath-like martensite into carbides occurred in the center of part of prior martensite (LM), and more tempered martensite (TM) in the FH-100 specimen; (3) the ferrite does not show clear thickening although more ferrite formed with extending holding time. Elemental distribution maps of C, Mn and Si corresponding to the scanning images of  Fig. 5 a and c shows banded segregations of manganese and silicon between the ferrite/martensite interfaces. That is, the ferrite forms preferentially along the rolling ferrite/pearlite interfaces. Extending the holding time at 1073 ​K favors the homogeneity; and (4) more secondary phases (RA and M/A islands) was observed in the FH-100 specimen. A schematic diagram is tentatively plotted to rationalize the phase transformation behavior, as shown in  Fig. 7 
                      . In the early fast-heating stage (below point  a  in  Fig. 4 b), a few ferrite recrystallizes from deformed ferrite and part of cementite starts to dissolve in the deformed pearlite. When the fast-heating starts above the  A c 1  (point  a  in  Fig. 4 b), austenization rapidly begins and completes once the temperature reaches above the  Ac 
                      3  (point  b  in  Fig. 4 b), accompanying with the disappear of ferrite. During the cooling from the peak temperature to the intercritical regime (from point  b  to  c  in  Fig. 4 b), new ferrite nucleates from austenite by austenite decomposition. Holding at the intercritical regime between point  c  and  d  in  Fig. 4 a, and subsequent cooling to lower temperature (point  e  in  Fig. 4 a) would lead to more ferrite formation by austenite decomposition. The residual austenite transforms to lath-like martensite with cooling below  M 
                      f  (point  e  in  Fig. 4 a). Overaging between point  f  and  g  in  Fig. 4 a for 300 ​s in the present study causes partial decomposition of lath-like martensite to tempered martensite. Different from the austenite nucleates and grows during the conventional intercritical isothermal annealing, almost all ferrite forms from prior austenite during the fast-heating annealing process. Ultrafine austenite grains may obtain during the early fast-heating stage, and thus promotes the formation of network ferrite by controlling austenite decomposition. A review on the mechanism of austenite decomposition during conventional annealing process has been summarized by Kumar et al. [ 36 ], where various nucleation sites, including grain corners, edges and boundaries were discussed, and the authors proposed besides the degree of undercooling (annealing temperature below the  Ac 
                      3 ), a critical grain size of austenite above 25 ​μm was important for the formation of network grain boundary ferrite (GBF). Similar interconnected network ferrite was obtained in the FH-100 specimen in the present work, as shown in  Fig. 5 c.

As discussed above, most of the ferrite firstly nucleates along the rolling ferrite/pearlite interfaces. With extending the holding time from 50 ​s to 100 ​s ​at 1073 ​K, newly-formed ferrite seems to appear by tearing the prior blocky austenite along the transverse direction. It is speculated that the nucleation plays an dominant role on the formation of ferrite during intercritical annealing, and the growth is suppressed to some extent since one cannot see obvious thickening of ferrite in the FH-100 specimen compared to that in the FH-50 specimen, which can also be reflected by the linear dilatometric curve during holding stage (between point  c  and  d  in  Fig. 4 a). Carbon content in martensite decreased with more time for elemental diffusion in the FH-100 specimen. Meanwhile, the elemental distributions of manganese and silicon become more homogeneous. However, incomplete martensitic transformation happens in part of austenite due to lower carbon content, and that is why more RA and/or M/A islands were observed in the FH-100 specimen. Additionally, lower carbon content in the center of martensite also favors the decomposition into carbides during the overaging stage at 513 ​K.

The measured mechanical properties for both groups of specimens are listed in  Table 2 
                      . The ultimate tensile strength (UTS) increased from 1190 ​MPa to 1204 ​MPa with extending the holding time from 50 ​s to 100 ​s ​at the intercritical temperature of 1073 ​K, and the fracture elongation improved from 13.3% to 16.7%. The results of Vickers hardness confirmed the reliability of UTS results to some extent, which was slightly higher than that in Ref. [ 37 ]. Generally, the UTS would decrease with the formation of more secondary phase and the martensite containing less carbon content; the slight enhancement of UTS of the FH-100 specimens was ascribed to the ultrafine microstructure. The enhanced fracture elongation can be well explained from the size discrepancy of fracture dimples, as shown in  Fig. 8 
                      , where a few cleavage features can be observed in FH-50 specimens (red arrows in  Fig. 8 a). Both groups of specimens underwent a void growth and coalesce, and rupture in ductile mode, and it appears that interconnected network ferrite in the FH-100 specimens can be more easily stretched by squeezing out the refined and discontinuous martensite. The UTS of both groups of fast-heating specimens is approximate 100 ​MPa higher than that of commercial DP980 steel produced through conventional annealing process (~1100 ​MPa [ 38 ]), and the elongation is comparative (~15.5% [ 38 ]) although they are not unsuitable to strictly compare due to the differences of gauge distance and sample dimensions for tensile testing. The present work proved the feasibility to produce high-performance dual-phase steel by means of fast-heating annealing method. Further work is needed to clarify the austenite decomposition mechanism, and the relationship between microstructure and mechanical properties is expected to be systematically established so as to better tailor microstructure to support industrial production.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: Fast-heating annealing process was applied to a commercially cold-rolled DP980 dual-phase steel in the present work and a phase transformation model was established to rationalize the microstructural evolution. It was proved that fast-heating annealing method provides a feasible way to produce high-performance dual-phase steels by taking advantage of austenite decomposition. When the cold-rolled DP980 steel sheet was fully austenitized at a heating rate of 300 ​K/s, ultrafine martensite surrounded by interconnected network ferrite can be obtained with a holding time of 100 ​s ​at 1073 ​K. The fracture elongation of the produced fast-heating DP980 dual-phase steel sheet enhanced up to 16.7% with an ultimate tensile strength of about 1200 ​MPa.
